I do · the big idea

What is a resource?

A resource is anything people use to satisfy their needs & wants. Environmental resources are the ones that come from nature.

💡 Light🌬️ Wind💧 Water🌱 Plants🪨 Rocks🐾 Animals

Which environmental resource did you use today?

The spheres are connected

I do · the key concept

Renewable vs Non-renewable

♻️ Renewable

Replenished as fast as we use them.

🌳 Trees💧 Water🌬️ Wind☀️ Sunlight
🛢️ Non-renewable

Limited, once they're gone, they're gone.

🪨 Coal🛢️ Oil🔥 Natural gas☢️ Uranium
Can renewables run out?

It depends how we use them

Even a renewable resource can run out if we use it too fast. Flip the switch and watch the forest.

Sustainable: only some trees are logged, so the forest regrows, it stays renewable forever.

🌲🌳🌲🌳🌲🌳 🚜 🌾 🌾 🌾
Non-renewable · drag through time

How fossil fuels form

Drag the slider through millions of years and watch dead plants become coal & oil. This is why they can't be replaced in our lifetime.

⛏️ Coal & oil!

🛢️ Fossil fuels

Coal, oil & natural gas, formed from buried plants & animals over millions of years of heat & pressure.

☢️ Nuclear

Uses uranium ore. Splitting atoms (fission) releases heat to make steam & electricity.

Another way to sort resources

Finite vs Infinite

♾️ Infinite

Sunlight & wind never run out on any human timescale.

⛏️ Finite
🪨🛢️

Coal, oil & lithium have a limit. Every use leaves less behind.

What kind of resource is water?

Renewable… but finite

♻️ Renewable

The water cycle and regular rainfall keep renewing our supply.

⛔ Finite

The total water on Earth never changes, so it's also limited. In long droughts it can even become temporarily non-renewable.

🏠 Domestic🌾 Agriculture🏭 Industry🌳 Environment🏊 Recreation

One river, six countries

Water is an interconnection, it links places & people. The Mekong River flows 0 km through six countries, carrying trade, food & life.

Lesson 5.3 · Water in Australia

Australia's
Water World

The location, distribution & variability of Australia's water, a land of droughts and flooding rains. Scroll to dive in. 🌊

🔎 Where is the water?🌏 Why so uneven?
Before we dive in · take a side 💬
"Australia is surrounded by ocean, so it can never run out of water."
👉 Now the tricky bit, be ready to explain why. What would a town actually need?
🌊 The ocean IS water, but it's salty. Turning seawater into drinkable water costs over $1 billion per plant and huge energy. So having water nearby isn't the same as being able to use it. What else might decide whether a place has enough water?

Turn to your partner: does living near lots of water always mean you'll never be thirsty? Explain why or why not.

Starter · guess first

The driest inhabited continent on Earth

Only Antarctica is drier. Guess how much rain falls across Australia in a year, then watch the number rise.

What do "droughts and flooding rains" tell us about Australia's water?

0
average rainfall a year, but some coasts get 3000 mm and the centre almost zero.

"…a land of droughts and flooding rains.", Dorothea Mackellar

Two kinds of water · tap to sort

Available or Potential?

Available water is easy & cheap. Potential water needs expensive tech. Tap each card.

Available water · surface

One country. Two rivers.

Surface water sits on the land, rivers, lakes & wetlands. But some flow all year, and some vanish. Flip the switch:

Perennial, always contains water. Example: the Blackwood River, SW WA.

Storing surface water

How big is a dam, really?

0 GL
Lake Argyle 🇦🇺
WA's largest
0 GL
Kariba Dam 🌍
Africa

Kariba holds about 17× more water. Dams also store water, stop floods & make hydro-electricity.

Environmental cost: dams block fish from breeding upstream (some go extinct), change water quality, trap sediment habitats need, and stop the natural floods that keep wetlands healthy.
Figure 5.3.5 The Gnangara system near Perth, three stacked aquifers.
Available water · underground

The hidden ocean below

Rain soaks in (infiltration) and is stored in porous rock, an aquifer. We pump it up through bores.

0
of Perth's water comes from underground. The Great Artesian Basin is the world's largest.
Potential water · unlocked with tech

When the easy water runs low

🌊 Desalination

Removes salt from seawater to make it potable. Reliable for dry coasts, but over $1 billion & huge energy. Plants in Perth, Sydney, Adelaide, Melbourne & Gold Coast.

♻️ Recycling

Cleans wastewater, even sewage, for crops, flushing & groundwater. Treated well it becomes potable, with no health problems ever recorded.

Tropical north
1000–2000+ mm. Monsoon rains, the wettest.
Far-north Qld
Up to 3000 mm, Australia's wettest.
South-west WA
~600–1000 mm, reliable winter rain.
The Red Centre
Under 200 mm, arid, the driest land.
South-east coast
~600–1000 mm, where most people live.
Distribution · make it rain 🌧️

Watch where the rain falls

The rain is falling live, heavy on the coasts, almost none in the centre. Tap a glowing pin to unleash a downpour & reveal that region's rainfall.

The pattern: coasts (north & east) are wettest; rain fades to the dry centre.
Figure 5.3.13 Australia's population density.
Distribution · people follow water

People live where the water is

Lay the rainfall & population maps together and a pattern jumps out.

A strong spatial association. High rain → lots of people (coasts & south-east). Dry centre → almost empty. Rivers follow the rain, draining through a drainage basin.
Fig 5.3.14 2008–2023 · blue = wet, red = dry.
Variability · never the same twice

Different every year

Most of Australia has four seasons, winter rain fills the dams. The tropical north has just two: a wet and a dry, with monsoons Oct–Apr.

Spot the very blue, wet 2011 and the very red, dry 2019. Can we ever rely on the rain?

Variability · long-term change

Climate change is moving the rain

Australia has warmed every decade since 1950, the hottest year was 2019.

0
South-west WA rain since 1970
0
South-east rain since 1994
0
Northern wet-season rain since 1994

And everywhere: more frequent, more intense droughts and floods.

Variability · humans change it

Cities break the water cycle

Compare the natural and urban cycles, flip the switch.

Rain soaks into soil (infiltration) and refills groundwater.

Lesson 8.4 · Investigating World War I

Where Australians
Fought

Gallipoli, Beersheba & the Western Front, the places, the sacrifice, and the birth of the Anzac legend. Scroll to begin. 🎖️

📍 Where did they fight?⭐ Why is it significant?📝 Notes to copy as we go
Before we begin · take a side 💬
"A country's proudest war memory is usually a big win. Australia's is a defeat, Gallipoli. Can a defeat be something to be proud of?"
👉 Be ready to explain why. What would make a defeat worth remembering?
▶ Choose a hook video (preview first)
  • DVA, “Gallipoli: The First Day”, 20-min animation, both Australian & Turkish sides.
  • The Cove, “Australia’s Gallipoli Campaign”, 14-min animated overview.
  • NMA, “The Anzacs at Gallipoli”, short, curriculum-aligned.
Our learning journey

What we're learning

✎ Learning intention
  • Understand where Australian men & women served in WWI, and why these places are historically significant.
  • Key concepts: significance · cause & effect · evidence · perspectives.
✎ Success criteria, I can…
  • name the key places (New Guinea, Gallipoli, Beersheba, Western Front)
  • explain what happened at Gallipoli & why it's remembered
  • describe the conditions soldiers faced
  • use evidence to explain significance
  • write a PEEL paragraph with dates & figures
A small nation, a huge sacrifice

Australia's contribution

0
troops sent overseas (from just ~7 million people)
0
Australians died · 210,000 casualties
0
only ~4,000 ever captured, they kept fighting
✎ Copy into your notes
  • Australia was small, only ~7 million people in 1917 (Germany 68m, Britain 46m).
  • It sent 331,781 troops overseas; 210,000 casualties; 61,519 died.
  • This was Australia's first war as a nation, its soldiers were recognised worldwide.
  • Still commemorated on Anzac Day (25 April) and Remembrance Day (11 November).
  • Significance = an event that led to change, marked a turning point, and is still remembered.
Australia acts immediately

Did Australia fire the first shot?

✎ Copy into your notes
  • 5 August 1914, hours after war was declared, the German ship SS Pfalz tried to flee Port Melbourne.
  • The commander of Fort Nepean (Victoria) ordered a warning shot across its bow.
  • The ship stopped and surrendered, described as the very first shot fired for the whole British Empire.
  • Cause & effect: Britain declares war → Australia is automatically at war too.
Australia's first campaign

German New Guinea (Aug–Sep 1914)

✎ Copy into your notes
  • German Admiral Spee's warships threatened Allied shipping in the South Pacific.
  • Australia's task, destroy the German radio stations & supply bases.
  • The Australian force landed at Rabaul (11 Sept 1914) and captured the radio station at Bita Paka.
  • Result, Australia captured the FIRST enemy territory of the entire war, and proved its forces could succeed.
The Ottoman Empire, c.1914
Why Egypt? What does 'Anzac' mean?

The birth of the Anzacs

✎ Copy into your notes
  • The Ottoman Empire (Türkiye) joined the Central Powers, blocking Allied aid to Russia via the Black Sea.
  • Britain also feared for its oil (Persia) and the vital Suez Canal.
  • Australian & NZ troops gathered in Egypt to train.
  • Oct 1914: 20,000 AIF + 10,000 NZ = the Australian & New Zealand Army Corps, led by Lt Gen Birdwood.
  • The acronym ‘ANZAC’ was first used in Cairo, early 1915.
The first fleet sails

Convoy 1 leaves Albany (1 Nov 1914)

Source 8.4.4 The AIF fleet departs King George Sound, Albany.
✎ Copy into your notes
  • The fleet gathered in King George Sound, Albany (WA).
  • 1 November 1914, 26 converted transport ships (plus warship escorts) set sail.
  • Almost 30,000 men and 8,000 horses made the slow journey to Egypt, then on to Gallipoli, the Middle East & the Western Front.
What did a soldier carry?

The kit of an Anzac

  • 🎩 Slouch hat, the iconic Australian hat
  • 🟫 Khaki uniform, to stay hidden in the Turkish sun
  • 🔫 Lee Enfield rifle + bayonet for close combat
  • 🥫 ~30 kg of rations, bully beef, hard biscuits, tea
  • 🎒 Sam Browne belt, compass, shovel, water bottle, ammo
  • 🦵 Puttees, cloth leggings wound up the leg
Gallipoli · part 1

Why invade Türkiye?

✎ Copy into your notes
  • The Ottomans secretly let German battleships into the Dardanelles waterway.
  • They closed it with mines and shelled Russian bases, cutting Russia off from supplies & ammunition.
  • Britain & France declared war on the Ottomans to reopen the route and help Russia.
  • The Western Front was a stalemate, commanders wanted a new way to break the deadlock.
  • Key place, the Dardanelles: a narrow sea passage linking the Mediterranean to the Black Sea.
Gallipoli · part 2

Churchill's naval plan fails

✎ Copy into your notes
  • Winston Churchill suggested sailing battleships into the Dardanelles to destroy the forts.
  • Weaknesses, British minesweepers were too weak against the current; the Turkish defences were underestimated.
  • 18 March 1915, several ships hit mines; the naval attack was called off. A disaster.
  • The navy then demanded army support → a land invasion was hastily planned.
  • Churchill was wrongly blamed for the land disaster too, and was demoted.
Anzac Cove
25 Apr 1915, the Anzacs landed 2 km off course.
Lone Pine
Aug 1915, 3 days of savage fighting; 7 VCs won.
The Nek
A hopeless charge, 234 Australians died in minutes.
The heights
The Turks held the high ground.
Gallipoli · part 3 · tap the pins 📍

The Anzac landing, 25 April 1915

✎ Copy into your notes
  • General Hamilton planned the invasion; he gave the Anzacs the ‘easier’ landing at Gaba Tepe.
  • He expected a quick 3-week victory, so ordered few doctors, nurses or medical supplies.
  • At dawn, 4,000 Australians landed first, but ~2 km off course, among the steep Sari Bair hills.
  • They were met with a hail of bullets. This beach became Anzac Cove.
Source 8.4.11 George Lambert's painting of the landing.
Gallipoli · part 4

The terrible first day

✎ Copy into your notes
  • The Turks were led by the brilliant Kemal Ataturk (later founder of modern Türkiye).
  • They defended their homeland fiercely from the high ground.
  • Officers were often killed first, leaderless groups pushed forward under fire.
  • By nightfall: ~3,000 Anzac casualties.
  • Hidden snipers dressed all in green shot Australians from behind (recalled by WA soldier Bert Facey).
Gallipoli · part 5

Conditions at Gallipoli

✎ Copy into your notes
  • 40,000 troops crammed into just 162 hectares, the size of a small dairy farm.
  • Steep terrain, carrying water, food & ammo up the ridges was harder than fighting.
  • No natural water at Anzac Cove, it came by ship in barrels; water was scarce & precious.
  • Poor toilets & disease everywhere.
  • About 50% of Anzac deaths were from DISEASE, not Turkish bullets.
Gallipoli · part 6

Resilience & the great battles

✎ Copy into your notes
  • Short of grenades, the Anzacs built a ‘bomb factory’, jam-tin bombs from cans, explosives & shrapnel.
  • Battle of Anzac (19 May 1915), 42,000 Turks charged 1,700 dug-in Anzacs; ~10,000 Turkish casualties; a ceasefire collected the wounded.
  • Battle of Lone Pine (6–9 Aug 1915), 3 days of hand-to-hand fighting; seven Victoria Crosses won.
  • Australians used periscopes to spot snipers without showing their heads.
  • Perspective: Turkish losses were often heavier, brave soldiers defending their homeland.
Source 8.4.21 A self-firing ‘drip rifle’.
Gallipoli · part 7 · a defeat, ended brilliantly

The silence ruse (Dec 1915)

0
troops evacuated in silence, with zero losses.
✎ Copy into your notes
  • General Brudenell White planned a secret, silent evacuation over five nights.
  • Wheels greased, horses fed, men whispered, self-firing ‘drip rifles’ tricked the Turks.
  • Gallipoli was a military defeat, but the escape was a masterpiece of planning.
⏱ 30-second check

Quick, can you answer?

1. What date was the Anzac landing?
2. Who commanded the Turkish forces?

25 April 1915 · Kemal Ataturk.

3. What caused ~half of all Anzac deaths?
4. What did the silence ruse achieve?

Disease · a silent evacuation of 105,000 men with no losses.
Source 8.4.27 The Australian Light Horse.
The Middle East · a bold victory

Beersheba, 1917

✎ Copy into your notes
  • The Turks were dug in with artillery set to a fixed range.
  • So the commander ordered the Light Horse to gallop FAST, past that range, bayonets drawn.
  • The guns couldn't re-aim in time, Beersheba fell with few casualties.
  • A clever, daring win, one of Australia's forgotten victories.
Fromelles
19–20 Jul 1916, worst 24 hrs in Australian history; 5,533 casualties.
Pozières
~23,000 casualties in 42 days.
Villers-Bretonneux
Apr 1918, halted the German offensive.
Hamel
Jul 1918, Monash's perfect victory.
Bigger than Gallipoli · tap the pins 📍

The Western Front

✎ Copy into your notes
  • Australia's actions in Europe were larger & more important than Gallipoli.
  • Pozières (1916), 19 attacks over 42 days; ~23,000 casualties. Bean: ‘more densely sown with Australian sacrifice than any place on earth’.
  • Fromelles (19–20 Jul 1916), a diversionary attack across open ground; 5,533 casualties, 1,719 killed in 24 hours.
Two men who changed the war, and how we remember it

Monash & Bean

✎ General John Monash
  • Australia's greatest general.
  • At Hamel (1918) he coordinated tanks, aircraft, artillery & infantry into one plan.
  • Montgomery called him “the best general on the Western Front.”
  • Monash University is named after him.
✎ Captain Charles Bean
  • The official war correspondent, an eyewitness at Gallipoli & the Western Front.
  • He turned history from simply recording events into careful investigation of evidence.
Check your understanding

Australian & New Zealand Army Corps.
Significancetap
Why an event matters / led to change.

A soldier killed, wounded or missing.
Silence rusetap
The silent evacuation of Gallipoli.

🎟️ Exit ticket · write in your notebook

Gallipoli was a defeat.
So why do we remember it so proudly?

Write one PEEL paragraph:

  • Point · Evidence (a fact/figure) · Explain · Link to significance.
Although Gallipoli was a defeat, Australians remember it proudly because of the courage and mateship the soldiers showed. For eight months the Anzacs held an impossible position with barely any water, and about half the deaths were from disease. This matters because their endurance, and the silent escape of 105,000 men without a single loss, showed extraordinary bravery and cleverness. For these reasons Gallipoli became a turning point that helped shape Australia's national identity, which is why it is still commemorated every Anzac Day.
🎖️

Lesson complete

You can now name where Australians fought, New Guinea, Gallipoli, Beersheba & the Western Front, and explain why these places are historically significant.

Sr. Yara · Year 9 History · Chapter 8.4 · Where Australians Fought 🎖️
Lesson 8.5 · Investigating World War I

Why Was WWI
So Destructive?

The trenches, the new weapons of the Industrial age, and the deadliest war the world had ever seen. Scroll to begin. ⚙️

⚙️ New weapons🕳️ Trench stalemate📝 Notes to copy as we go
Before we begin · take a side 💬
"New technology usually makes life better. In WWI it made war deadlier than ever. Is human invention always a good thing?"
👉 Be ready to explain why. Can you think of an invention that did both harm and good?
▶ Choose a hook video (preview first)
  • History Bombs, “Why Were the Weapons of WWI So Deadly?”, fun, animated, school-safe.
  • IWM, Trench Warfare, clips + stories from real soldiers.
  • Britannica, WWI trench warfare on the Western Front.
Our learning journey

What we're learning

✎ Learning intention
  • Understand why WWI was so much more destructive than earlier wars, and the conditions soldiers faced.
  • Key concepts: cause & effect · continuity & change · significance · evidence.
✎ Success criteria, I can…
  • explain how the war changed from movement to trench stalemate
  • describe trench-warfare conditions
  • define war of attrition, total war & shell shock
  • explain how new industrial weapons made the war so deadly
  • use figures as evidence in an argument
‘Home by Christmas’

The illusion of a short war

✎ Copy into your notes
  • In 1914 people imagined war like old paintings, heroic cavalry charges, splendid uniforms, glory.
  • Everyone assumed it would be over in a few months.
  • They were wrong, new weapons multiplied the ability to kill a thousandfold.
  • Worse weapons followed: poison gas and flamethrowers.
  • Continuity & change: soldiers & rifles continued, but industrial-scale killing changed everything.
A fast start… then deadlock

The Schlieffen Plan & the stalemate

1914, Germany's Schlieffen–Moltke Plan: beat France fast (through neutral Belgium) before Russia mobilises.
Sept 1914, the French stop Germany at the Battle of the Marne.
Late 1914, both sides dig in. The ‘war of movement’ becomes a ‘war of entrenchment’.
Result, trench warfare. Cavalry is now useless.
✎ Amazing but true
  • France had too few trucks, so the government ordered every taxi in Paris to drive soldiers to the front, some drivers even switched on the meter!
Source 8.5.8 Two opposing trench lines, with no man's land between.
The landscape of death

Building the trenches

✎ Copy into your notes
  • Trenches stretched ~750 km, Belgian coast to Switzerland. In total ~2,490 km were dug by hand.
  • Built by sapping (digging), tunnelling and sandbagging; ~3 m deep, 2 m wide.
  • Layers: front-line → support → reserve → communication trenches.
  • Between the two sides lay no man's land, an open killing ground.
‘Hell on Earth’

Conditions in the trenches

✎ Copy into your notes
  • Lice infested every uniform, constant misery.
  • Rats spread disease and fed on the dead.
  • Armies lost almost as many men to illness as to fighting.
  • Deep, sticky mud could be deadly, at Passchendaele men drowned in it.
Source 8.5.18 A soldier at Passchendaele, 1917.
Three deadly ideas

New words for a new war

Static warfare

Armies sit in fixed positions. Thousands could die without capturing even 1 metre.

War of attrition

You can't win outright, so you wear the enemy down by killing as many as possible.

Total war

War spreads beyond the battlefield, bombing cities, controlling factories, food & news.

✎ Copy into your notes
  • Static warfare, fixed positions; huge losses for almost no ground.
  • War of attrition, victory = when the enemy can't replace its soldiers.
  • Total war, Zeppelins bombed English towns; governments used censorship & controlled factories.
The hidden wounds

Shell shock & the people behind the lines

✎ Copy into your notes
  • Endless bombardment damaged men's minds, Dr Charles Myer named it ‘shell shock’.
  • By 1916, over 40% of casualties were believed to be suffering from it.
  • It was not understood, sufferers were often wrongly called cowards.
  • Women served too, ~3,000 Australian nurses abroad; 29 died, often close to the firing line.
0
of casualties by 1916 were believed to suffer shell shock.
Slaughter for almost nothing

The killing battles of 1916–17

0
French casualties at Verdun
0
≈ casualties at the Somme
0
British casualties on the first day of the Somme
✎ Copy into your notes
  • Verdun (1916), huge German attack on France; French ~550,000 & German ~430,000 casualties; French troops even mutinied.
  • The Somme (1916), British–French attack; ~1 million casualties; British lost 57,000 (19,240 killed) on day one, their worst day ever.
  • Passchendaele / 3rd Ypres (1917), sank into a death-trap of mud; remembered with horror.
  • Hundreds of thousands died, yet the front line barely moved (a ‘war of attrition’).
Source 8.5.23 Deaths per day across 10 major wars.
Look at the numbers

The deadliest war yet

0
deaths every single day, far higher than any war before, nearly 3× the next-deadliest.

A single figure like this is powerful evidence, quote it to prove how destructive WWI was.

When industry went to war

The technologies of death

The Industrial Revolution mass-produced deadlier versions of old weapons, and invented terrifying new ones.

💥 Heavy artillery🔫 Machine gun☠️ Poison gas🔥 Flamethrowers🛡️ Tanks✈️ Aircraft🌊 Submarines🎯 Snipers
✎ Copy into your notes
  • Artillery caused most casualties, hundreds of shells an hour.
  • The machine gun mowed down whole lines of men in seconds.
  • New horrors: poison gas, flamethrowers, tanks, aircraft & submarines.
  • Cause & effect: the urgent need to WIN pushed technology forward at frightening speed, making the war far more destructive.
The conflict spreads

One war, many fronts

✎ Copy into your notes
  • Western Front (France & Belgium), the main trench line, the deadliest fighting.
  • Eastern Front, Russia fought bravely but, poorly supplied, suffered catastrophic losses and collapsed.
  • Dardanelles Front, Gallipoli was just one part.
  • Middle East, Australians (the Light Horse) fought from Gaza to Beersheba, guarding vital oil.
  • Italian & Balkan Fronts, the war spread across Europe. This was ‘total war’.
1918, the tide turns

How the war ended

1917, the USA joins the Allies, eventually sending 2 million troops + huge industrial power.
1918, Germany's last ‘Spring Offensive’ fails; the British blockade starves German cities.
Allies counter-attack, including Monash's Australians, and break through.
11 a.m., 11 Nov 1918, an armistice ends the fighting. We mark it every Remembrance Day.
✎ Copy into your notes, the aftermath
  • Peace was settled at the Treaty of Versailles, near Paris.
  • PM Billy Hughes demanded Australia a seat: “I speak for 60,000 dead. How many do you speak for?”
  • Australia gained a mandate over German New Guinea (until PNG independence in 1975).
  • The harsh treaty punished Germany, causing hardship that helped the Nazis rise and led to WWII.

Key terms

The deadly open ground between the trench lines.
Stalematetap
Neither side can win, both dig in.

Wearing the enemy down by killing as many as possible.
Total wartap
War that targets civilians & whole economies.
Shell shocktap
Mental trauma from constant bombardment.

An agreement to stop fighting (11 Nov 1918).

🎟️ Exit ticket · write in your notebook

Why was World War I so much more
destructive than earlier wars?

Write one PEEL paragraph: Point · Evidence (a figure!) · Explain · Link to cause & effect.

World War I was so much more destructive than earlier wars mainly because of the new industrial weapons and the deadly stalemate of trench warfare. Machine guns and heavy artillery could kill hundreds in minutes, and because neither side could break through, the war became a “war of attrition”, about 5,509 people died every day, with nearly a million casualties at the Somme alone. This kept the killing going for over four years, and new weapons like gas and tanks made it worse. It shows how a change in technology completely changed the nature of war.
🎖️
